assigned for the privacy of the prisoners and their wives. He

H

— صفحة 124 —

Occasional Marital Privacy for Prisoners

123

paced slowly back and forth, back and forth, until visiting

time was over, and the prisoners went back to their

dormitories. Then he assembled the wardens and addressed

them in a stern, commanding tone, ‘I, the manager of the

citadel and the prison, have just done your job… the work

of the prison warder, and I was proud to do it… I was

happy to do what’s right and to help these couple to avoid

forbidden acts. From this day on whoever refuses to

perform this duty will be strictly penalized.

‘Why do you regard this humane indulgence, which

Al’lah has legalised, with contempt? Maybe the husband

needs his wife to repair his clothes or to discuss private

family matters which they did not want the other prisoners

or the jailers to overhear.’

With that, a normal routine was established and they

went back to fulfilling this humane assignment, willingly or

unwillingly, because they had seen that the commander had

shown the way and not been too proud to undertake the

job himself.

Officer Mohammad Emin had understood the positive

effects of that humane service through his great insight and

his illumination by Al’lah’s Light, for there are family

matters between a husband and his wife which the prisoner

cannot discuss within the sight or hearing of other people

present during the communal visit.

Besides, this deed of Officer Sheikho does not conflict

with the reason that reformative prisons were established,

— صفحة 125 —

Stories of the Scholar

124

nor does it disagree with Godly Mercy. In fact, a point that

many people forget is that the prison was originally

established with the aim of reforming men found guilty of

crime, and not for destroying their families and human

spirits.

And what is more, not allowing a prisoner to be alone

with his wife for a short while can cause moral deterioration,

and a terrible lowering of both morals and religious belief,

and in many cases, even sexual deviation and the spread of

sodomy among the prisoners. On the other hand, this simple

connection helps the prisoners to avoid such ugly aberrations

and also stops their wives from straying and being tempted

to commit adultery during their husbands’ absence and

period of incarceration. It builds up hope in their spirits and

maintains a strong bond between the prisoner and his family

whereby he fully realises the happiness created within the

family unit and, hopefully, stops committing any further

crimes or disgraceful deeds, and making it so much easier for

him to truly repent.

— صفحة 126 —

125

The Irreverent Grocer Is Foiled

“Truly, the eyes may commit adultery by looking.”

ou may wonder, why the Almighty orders us to lower

our gaze. We know that adultery is a dangerous

social aberration. When it becomes widespread in

society, that society will crumble and be destroyed just as the

AIDS syndrome devastates a man’s body, rendering it

powerless and subject to the slightest infection which will

cause it to waste away, depleted and destroyed by the power

of the infection.

That critical illness breaks down even the most hallowed

social links, as when the first basic cell in the structure of

society, the family, deteriorates, it will collapse and be

completely destroyed; this is contrary to the bond of marriage

which is based upon a proper foundation and the strict rules

enacted for us by our Wise and Omniscient Creator.

The fruits of adultery may well be a generation of

illegitimate children since there will be no father to

acknowledge them, or raise and advise them, therefore they

will follow the ways of corruption and wrongdoing through

delinquency. Furthermore, it is important to consider the

Y

— صفحة 127 —

Stories of the Scholar

126

perilous future which the adulteress would suffer, for the

adulterer would surely desert her in favour of another

woman after her first flush of beauty has waned, leaving her

desolate when subjected to the pursuant misery and

destitution of her horrible, dreary fate.

And so it is with him, for when he deserts the material life

he will have left behind no lasting benefits to society; on the

contrary, he will be exposed to the pernicious ailment which

arises from such a course. He will be like a destructive

pickaxe demolishing the happiness of every woman he may

connect with, and at the end of his lifetime he will find no

loving child or kindly relative to help him in the twilight of

his years. He will certainly suffer from sorrow and burn with

misery at the lamentable end of his life. Even if he seeks

marriage towards the end of his youth, he will undoubtedly

select a maiden since he will have become accustomed to

connecting with young girls. Moreover, he will be unlikely

to settle for just one woman as he has been used to drinking

from different springs, and so his wife might also react to his

errant ways after he reaches middle age.

Consequently, problems such as boredom and weariness

would arise on both sides, quite apart from the physical

diseases stemming from this lowly path which are obvious

to everyone; this state often results in divorce. Therefore,

and to turn mankind away from following such a course,

the Almighty legislates the law for him, since Al’lah’s

Religion is a religion of preservation, and as the saying goes,

— صفحة 128 —

The Irreverent Grocer Is Foiled

127

“Prevention is better than cure.” The Almighty says, “Nor

come close to adultery”, that is, anything may lead one to

commit fornication: speech, song, shaking hands, cinema,

radio, looking at women. Just as the eye may provoke

adultery, it is the same with the ear and the hand; and all of

this may lead man to commit fornication. God continues,

“For it is indecent and a bad path.”

1 It leads man to have

his offspring through a contemptible way and causes harm

to those who commit it.

Al’lah had revealed this wisdom and requested that all

mankind should apply this teaching voluntarily, since he

who does not comply with it will be ruined. The Almighty

shows us that following these unequivocal verses which

reveal to us the way to achieve our happiness, will result in

our bliss here on this earth and in the Hereafter, when we

are amongst the dwellers of Heaven. The Almighty orders

us, “Tell the men who are believers that they should

lower their gaze and guard their modesty: that will make

for greater purity for them; and Al’lah is Well-

Acquainted with all that they do.”

2

According to this verse, Al’lah commands us to lower our

gaze because the eye can commit adultery simply by looking

and then forming impure thoughts; and if a man fails to lower

his gaze he will fall into the ways of fornication and lose his

discretion. On the contrary, by lowering and averting his sight

1 The Holy Qur’an, Fortress (Surah) 17, The Night Journey (al-Isra’), verse 33.

2 The Holy Qur’an, Fortress (Surah) 24, Light (al-Nur), verse 30.

— صفحة 129 —

Stories of the Scholar

128

he will guard his modesty and he will be preserved from

falling into the sinful ways of fornication. If he consistently

lowers his gaze he will maintain his modesty and love his wife

and she, too, will love him.

If mankind does not apply this Instruction given by Al’lah,

the Almighty will send them warnings, and cautions, or inflict

hardship or distress so that they may understand the error of

their ways which lead man to commit fornication.

This incident which occurred with the grocer who rented

a shop from Mohammad Emin is a perfect explanation for

the saying mentioned above.

Mohammad Emin had inherited this old shop from his

late father, and it was situated on the ground floor of the

house where the master lived with his small family. The

house consisted of two floors, the upper one occupied by

the highly-principled man, Mohammad Emin, and his

family, and the ground floor which included the shop.

Usually, as Emin Bey passed by, he would see the grocer

sitting on a chair at the door of the shop with an open copy

of the Holy Qur’an resting in his hands. One would assume

that this indicated moral rectitude and presaged that his

conduct and behaviour would inevitably conform to the true

religion in relation to trustworthiness. Of course, all of this

was most desirable if that grocer really had been truly faithful

and honest, or even sought Al’lah’s Satisfaction.

But, alas… the reality was different, and as one knows,

appearances can be deceptive, which has been proven by

— صفحة 130 —

The Irreverent Grocer Is Foiled

129

fact. It happened one day when the great guide was passing

in front of the shop and noticed the grocer’s eyes chasing

what Al’lah had forbidden: he was lost in his devilish

thoughts and gazing lustfully at a woman walking past the

shop, his eyes following her till she faded in the distance.

And yet he held the Holy Qur’an open in his hands and

then turned back to studying it for all to observe!

And now, in an instant, our great guide had seen him for

what he really was: the shopkeeper had fallen into the sin of

staring at what Al’lah had forbidden, which would inevitably

lead him to something even worse, that is to commit

adultery. That honourable man, Mohammad Emin Sheikho,

objected to seeing this infringement not only in his

neighbourhood, but in his very own shop. He felt a surge of

Godly Anger, full of mercy, flowing into every atom of his

spirit, mixed with sorrow for this sinner and for the misery

he would bring upon himself. This is why he hurried to

admonish the shopkeeper so that he might reflect on his

mistake and withdraw from his straying and carelessness.

Our man hoped that he would convince him to realise the

error of his ways and come to his senses to escape from the

possible results of this deed, and from the devil’s snares, and

avoid the unhappiness and pains he would ultimately incur

for himself.

He went up to the shopkeeper and said to him, ‘What

have you just done? Is this allowed? Isn’t it incompatible with

religion and morals… and with honesty and uprightness?’

chapters.title: صفحة 131 - 140 (Stories of the Scholar)
chapters.html:
— صفحة 131 —

Stories of the Scholar

130

Knowing full well what that honest man meant, the wily

tradesman replied, ‘What do you mean, Bey?’

The merciful master said, ‘I have seen you looking

openly at women… is that acceptable?’

The sly shopkeeper replied, ‘But, surely we’re allowed to

look just once… but any further glances will count against

us!’

Emin Bey said to him, ‘But it was a long gaze, in fact it

took your entire attention. You literally swallowed her with

your eyes… Look, man, the eye may commit adultery just by

looking, and you are falling deeper into this shameful act…

into immorality… I’m telling you now in case you didn’t

realise it, otherwise it would be better if you stop sitting there

with the Holy Qur’an in your hands, pretending piety and

righteousness. As long as you display such hideous deed you

may give the wrong impression about the religion. And what’s

more, I’m also telling you that the man that is not a strong

believer may suppose that your behaviour represents true

religion and that all religious men are like you… so, you will

only misrepresent and debase the religion and its beliefs.’

One day, not long after this incident, Mohammad Emin

happened to notice that a man went into the grocery shop

to buy a few items, which he paid for according to the

prices shown. Shortly after the man left with his purchases

a little girl came in and, by the Wisdom of the Wise, she

bought sweet melon for which the stated price was one

franc for a kilogram. But the grocer lied and told her that it

— صفحة 132 —

The Irreverent Grocer Is Foiled

131

was two francs for the kilo, that is, he charged her double

the price… yes, he had traded on this child’s tender years to

make a greater profit.

At this, the spirit of our honest man rebelled: he felt as if

every particle of his being was rejecting the state of affairs

concerning that dishonest and corruptive man who had

withdrawn far from Al’lah. What fate would he face in this

life before the heavenly life to come, if he never retreated

from his wrongful ways, came to his senses and duly

repented?

Mohammad Emin began to chastise him, pointing out

the error of his ways, and described to him the gravity of

his straying from the right path, so that he might discard

the cloak of depravity and Satanism and replace it with the

garment of humanity for which he had been born. He said

to him, ‘Why did you do that, man? Would you sell your

eternal life for this despicable way of life… because you’re

earning your daily bread through unlawful means? Isn’t this

deceit? Even though the Prophet (cpth) said, “He who

cheats can never belong to us”, I saw you take extra

money from that innocent child, so tell me isn’t that theft

or even usury? Don’t you know that Al’lah abhors it and

will ensure that money gained in this way will be lost; and

yet He blesses the money given as alms? Won’t you die one

day? Do you think this world will last forever? How will

you face your Provider, you who pretend to be so pious and

upright? What state will you be in?’

— صفحة 133 —

Stories of the Scholar

132

But insisting on his errant ways and following his

whims, the heartless tradesman replied, ‘Oh, Bey! It’s called

trade and trade is based upon craftiness!’

Hereupon, Mohammad Emin realised that such a man

would never respond to his admonishments because he was

bent on his life of depravation, swindling and pretence. He

acted like an infectious disease which would inflict illness

on the human body, and when transmitted would impose

grave danger on the whole of society.

That is why this virtuous and noble master decided that

he ought to tell the underhand merchant to vacate the

shop, since he understood full well that gentle words would

achieve nothing with him. So, the only solution was for

him to leave not only the shop but also the neighbourhood,

therefore our honest man felt that he should admonish him

directly and forcefully. So he said, ‘Listen to me, man! I

don’t want to see you here tomorrow… get out of my shop

today or else I’ll have to treat you severely… and I don’t

want to be forced into it… have you understood?’

When the sly shopkeeper heard these words, his heart was

overcome with fear; he trembled with terror when he saw

this august master appear like a predatory and rapacious lion

which it would be foolish to confront. The shopkeeper’s

strength failed him and he remained silent. Then he said, ‘At

the end of this month, before the rent is due again, I shall

empty the shop for you.’ Mohammad Emin departed having

warned the tradesman that he would hold him to his word.

— صفحة 134 —

The Irreverent Grocer Is Foiled

133

That night, a fire broke out in the grocery store and as

soon as Mohammad Emin realised what was happening, he

dashed down to help to put it out. He rushed out of his

house like a whirlwind and found some of the neighbours

had quickly gathered to extinguish the fire. It was too late

as the flames had incinerated all the goods in the shop

leaving nothing but cinders, but strangely enough there was

no damage to the wooden ceiling above which was the floor

of the honourable master’s house. The reason for this can

easily be explained: the source of money from which alms

has been paid will never be destroyed.

A fire engine arrived on the scene soon after the fire had

been extinguished and a police car went to the grocer’s house

to tell him what had happened. No-one had witnessed the

occurrence the previous day or overheard Mohammad Emin

ordering the grocer to vacate the shop. At that point,

extinguishing the fire and the losses of the poor grocer were

uppermost on everyone’s minds and there was no suspicion

at all as to who might have caused the fire: certainly no-one

would have suspected Mohammad Emin.

At the grocer’s home, the policemen knocked at the

door, waking him from his sleep. When they informed him

of the fire, the news came like a bolt from the bluel; he

cried, ‘Oh… Oh, no! It’s my own fault… yes, by God, I

forgot my cigarette on the block of fat. Oh, what terrible

luck! Has everything been destroyed? My losses will be

enormous if all my goods have been burnt.’

— صفحة 135 —

Stories of the Scholar

134

He kept crying and, in his anguish, repeating himself

over and over again, wringing his hands in despair.

In fact, in his distress he was unaware that he was uttering

the truth: Al’lah had made him say these words which would

acquit the noble master of any wrongdoing, since the

suspicion might well have focused on him.

Before the shopkeeper could even think about the

previous day’s incident and make use of it maliciously to

take revenge by accusing Mohammad Emin of purposely

starting the fire, he unwittingly spoke the truth about the

cause of the fire. So, he had no chance of changing his

mind and accusing him since he had confessed the truth in

front of the policemen.

As for the faithful wife of Mohammad Emin, that

merciful, tender-hearted mother, she became extremely

troubled when she heard about the accident, because of her

great concern for her children, especially when she saw the

flames and smoke rising from the ground floor and coming

through the window. The actual situation, though, was not

as bad as she thought. This Wise Godly Measure included

His great Goodness for her and for her honest and pure

husband, as due to extreme fear for her two sons, she hurried

to their room thinking to carry them out to the street; but in

her anxiety she forgot to cover her face with her veil and

failed to put on her black cape. And yet, the High

Omnipotent God arranged a solution… with a difference!

Since she was good-hearted and pure, Al’lah preserved

her from harm in this dangerous situation because she was

— صفحة 136 —

The Irreverent Grocer Is Foiled

135

horrified and overwhelmed with the fear that her sleeping

children might be burnt to death. So, being unable to carry

both boys at the same time she quickly carried one of them

to another room; but instead of putting him down and

returning empty-handed to bring the second child she

forgot to put down the first child and he was still in her

arms as she went back to get the second son. Such was her

state of distress that she put him back where she had taken

him from and picked up the second child to remove him to

safety in the opposite room. This state of confusion

continued for some time as she ran back and forth between

the two rooms, moving first one child and then the other,

unable to pick up both of them together… her distress

mounting with every passing moment as she was convinced

that her sons would be harmed.

Finally, the matter came to an end and the fire was put

out. When the honest master returned to his house he found

her still overcome with worry and entirely exhausted. So, he

calmed her fears and told her that the fire had been

extinguished without causing any damage to the ceiling of the

shop (which was directly below the floor of the house) and

that the danger was over, and everything would be fine. In his

gentle way he was able to reassure her and she soon returned

to her normal tranquil self for the sake of their children.

So, God’s Mercy is given specifically to those who need

it, as is His Affliction, as everyone receives what he deserves

according to his intentions and deeds whether they be good

— صفحة 137 —

Stories of the Scholar

136

or bad. If a man intends goodness he will find nothing but

goodness, and if he commits evil deeds, he will be afflicted

with punishment and chastisement here on this earth and

in the Hereafter unless he shows true repentance and

returns to his right mind.

Thus, the Wisdom and Compassion of the Wise and

Merciful Al’lah were pleased to release this merciful man,

Mohammad Emin, who was not accustomed to giving way

to lies and leaving them to circulate. On the contrary, he

always quashed them most forcefully. Similarly with the

residents of the quarter, when they became comfortable with

that licentious, depraved and corruptive man, Al’lah rid

them of his wrongdoing by imposing appropriate sanctions

so that he might learn to refrain from his careless perfidy,

come back to his right mind and correct his sinful ways

before it became too late and he forfeited his eternal life. On

the other hand, Al’lah had protected our virtuous and pure

master, and his wife, from every evil, when the ceiling of the

shop was not damaged and prevented her from going out,

unveiled, to the street and erroneously show herself to the

people outside.

Al’lah had saved her and her honest husband from that

difficult situation in order to preserve the purity of them

both, and for the honour of her great husband (God

sanctified his lofty secret and eternal support).

— صفحة 138 —

137

Prisoner in the Castle

or Guest of Honour?

he incidents described here took place when Officer

Mohammad Emin held the position of director of

Damascus Castle during the French Mandate over

Syria. This vast castle contained an extensive prison full of

those who had broken the law, and arsenals stocked with

large amounts of weapons and military equipment belonging

to the French government which ruled our countries at that

time. So, the preparation for war and equipping the armies

with war material and provisions were managed in this castle

by its director-general Mohammad Emin Sheikho. He was

in charge of all its departments and affairs and therefore

responsible for despatching the troops from there.

As one can see, our officer held a considerable post in

the government, and a castle of such importance should

definitely be directed by a man who was worthy of having

such a high level of responsibility and trust placed in his

hands. Therefore, our officer was always charged with those

weighty, critical tasks which required a strong character and

great wisdom and acumen to fulfill them successfully.

T

— صفحة 139 —

Stories of the Scholar

138

The ruling class at that time would resort to him for

help with the many varied problems which they were

unable to solve, whether within the castle or beyond its

walls, and indeed in all of Damascus. Needless to say, our

officer resolved all problems perfectly. Therefore they called

him ‘Aslan’

1, a nickname by which he had long been

known, because of their affection for him and their

admiration of his humane accomplishments and his great

integrity: it was as if he was the leader and they were his

followers.

For this reason, there were many men who were jealous

and harboured feelings of ill-will towards him. They did

not like his truthfulness and loyalty so they did their best to

destroy the man who stood as a stronghold against the

tottering towers of their disbelief and transgressions, and

eradicated their dreams and greed, thus putting an end to

the outcomes of their evil and wrongful deeds. They

constantly tried to undermine his excellent character by

spreading doubts about his honesty and his capacity to be

the director, and hatching all manner of plots against him.

Had he fallen foul of even one of those plots, his fate would

have been either exile or capital punishment. But the

Almighty was always his Protector. He supported him by

giving him power and authority and directed him towards

1 Aslan is a Turkish word that means ‘the lion’. The Turkish senior

commanders gave the officer Mohammad Emin Sheikho this epithet for the

awesome qualities of boldness, courage and intrepidity they saw in him; and it

was the name they used among themselves.

— صفحة 140 —

Prisoner in the Castle or Guest of Honour?

139

the performing of good deeds and successful tasks that

helped to protect him and maintain his prestige.

This story demonstrates to us a lamentable fact which

affirms that the man who turns away from God will live in

constant misery and darkness. He will spend his life as

though blind and deaf, unable to see the light or hear the

truth, until he ends up at a level lower than that of an

animal and more distant than that of the devil; unless my

Lord should feel fit to bestow His Mercy.

One of the adjutants who worked with Officer Mohammad

Emin is an example: his heart became entirely controlled by

the devil when he adopted a hostile attitude towards our

officer. The devil began to support him in weaving schemes

and plots against the honest officer, and making his bad deeds

and wrongdoing seem right and fair to him. He also raised in

him false hopes for a life full of fulfillment and glory, but one

achieved in entirely the wrong way. Thus, this man became a

real source of evil and began to spread corruption throughout

the land by any means possible. Step by step, he gave himself

up to the devil and turned into a weapon in the demon’s

hands to fulfill his purpose in misleading the sons of Adam

and driving them away from the sources of good, truth and

honest pleasure. The adjutant’s heart became a mass of bitter

rancour and hatred.

Whenever he saw anyone enjoying some special favour,

he wanted to have it for himself; in fact, he wished to

possess everything the earth had to offer in the way of

chapters.title: صفحة 141 - 150 (Stories of the Scholar)
chapters.html:
— صفحة 141 —

Stories of the Scholar

140

pleasure, grace and treasure, so as to use or dispose of it

however he wished. His self-love was paramount to him; he

could not deprive himself of its low desires which

overwhelmed him and settled in his debased heart. As a

result, he lived in absolute darkness and his heart grew ever

darker until eventually he came to loathe kindness and

goodwill. His worldly desires obscured the light which

enabled him to see the truth, so he became unable to

distinguish between good and evil, and never hesitated to

fulfill all that his sick whims and impulses desired.

‘Why not? Why couldn’t I be the overlord of this

generation? Couldn’t I become a famous personality whose

name will go down in history? But what about that man,

Officer Sheikho? He puts me in the shade. His character and

abilities are far superior and greater than mine. He’s the only

obstacle standing in my way. I shall do whatever it takes to

destroy him. I’m so envious of all that he has and is!’

This man then took full advantage of every opportunity

that presented itself to defame the character of Officer

Mohammad Emin whom he believed stood in the way of

his future development and happiness. So, he became

preoccupied with telling lies and making up false

accusations about him, in an attempt to slander his habitual

honesty and the purity of his good name. Because of his

insistence on evil, Al’lah the Almighty actually gave him the

power to bring out the mean wishes which filled his spirit

and were written on his heart, and so he wandered too far

— صفحة 142 —

Prisoner in the Castle or Guest of Honour?

141

off the right path. He lived in an ivory palace built by his

own dreams and covetousness, which had taken control of

him, and which he believed would raise him to a high

position of authority and glory.

Nevertheless, the Will of God (Glory to His Names) and

the rule of compassion which He decreed Himself and

which overwhelms all His creatures, prescribed the help

these people needed to turn away from this terrible path

which would lead them to a horrible end at the time of

their death. His Clemency and Tenderness require that

anyone that mistakes his own goodness should be alerted to

the error of his ways and warned of the outcomes of his

tyranny which will cause him nothing but failure and

misery, surely to be followed by total loss and remorse.

Therefore He directs distress and misfortune towards him

in order to turn him from his lowly desires and whims. If

he, when calamity strikes, realises his sins and the enormity

of the error of his ways, he should then resort to God and

pray to him truthfully. He would then advance on a

journey of repentance seeking God’s Forgiveness, by being

attached to the cords of sincerity which would reveal to him

the reality of this world and the dirtiness of his deeds, as

they would acquaint him with God’s Mercy and abundant

Favour given to him and, indeed, to all His creatures.

That is what happened with the adjutant of whom we

speak, whose greediness and shunning of what is right, grew

until the desire for the material things of life captivated his

— صفحة 143 —

Stories of the Scholar

142

heart, so he mounted the wings of his imagination and

instead of soaring high as a bird, he descended from one level

of darkness to another, all the while thinking that he could

reach the moon and become the focus of all eyes. But

suddenly, his self-conceit broke, his pride vanished, and his

ivory palace fell down around him, throwing him into a

bottomless pit. He was hoisted with his own petard. The

arrow which he had fired to hit the great heart of this officer

turned back to hit him, even though that heart of that officer

wished for him nothing but good and prayed only for his

proper guidance and infinite happiness in this world and the

world to come.

He said to himself, ‘Woe betide me! Soon I’ll be

captured by Officer Sheikho; I have no pistol and am

powerless… I’ll surely be convicted because of my crime

and evil deeds. What’s more, I was hostile towards him and

lost no opportunity to speak badly about him. Oh, I wish I

had the power to kill him! But no! I will not give in to fear

and desperation. I have to persevere and screw up my

courage to be able to meet him and face up to his assault.’

And so, that disastrous night, when that miserable man

was arrested in the very act, was the worst night of his life.

He was taken to a filthy, dark cell in the police station

before being driven to the prison in Damascus Castle to

spend the period of his sentence. There were many

hundreds of prisoners and criminals in that huge prison,

criminals who had been brought from all parts of the

Damascus region and its environs.

— صفحة 144 —

Prisoner in the Castle or Guest of Honour?

143

The time dragged by so slowly as he sat miserably in the

middle of the room on a rickety wooden bench covered

with a dirty, worn rug. A dim light penetrated the only

filthy window high in the wall, drawing on the ground the

fearful black shadow of a prisoner; outside could be heard

the sound of the slow, measured footfall of the guard who

paced back and forth. In his isolation, this sound unnerved

him and roused him to a violent reaction within himself.

An icy coldness began to creep into his bones. It was the

coldness of his feelings of loneliness, and his fear of the

approaching hardships which he anticipated living under,

and in which he felt as though he were about to be buried

alive. His teeth chattered and his body trembled as he

looked at his feet and almost felt the severe pains he would

suffer. He imagined them swollen and encircled by drops of

his own warm blood, and a cold sweat broke out on his

pale forehead. His black shadow drawn on the floor of the

cell reminded him of his dark, churlish deeds and a loud

cry issued from him and resounded in the room, ‘Go away!

I don’t want to see you. Go away, you cursed blackness.

You remind me of myself. I’m suffering enough distress.’

That is the state of anyone who shuns God. His dark

deeds cling to him like a shadow, depriving him of sleep

and embittering his life. They keep reminding him of the

blackness of his heart and the darkness of his grave.

The prisoner had no relief from this state until eventually

he became exhausted by his imagination and obsessed by

— صفحة 145 —

Stories of the Scholar

144

his fear of the suffering to come. So, he lay down trying to

relax… trying to sleep so that he might forget the situation

he was in and the horrible visions which shared his

loneliness and did away with his peace and tranquillity. But

as soon as he closed his eyes, he felt as though he were being

whipped severely without mercy; so he started trembling and

moved away from that ill-omened bench. He looked

around the room but found no-one except that accursed

black shadow. He talked to it, but it gave no reply. He

shouted at it, but in vain. So, he decided to ignore it and

began to walk around the cell, dragging his tired legs, trying

to brace his spiritual powers in order to stay firm and not to

break down.

‘Oh God! What’s the matter with me? Have I lost my

mind? Couldn’t I stay strong and control myself? I

shouldn’t care about being sentenced to a term in prison.

Imprisonment denotes manhood. I counted all the costs

before I committed that crime, so I was fully aware of the

possible consequences and knew that if I was found out I

would be arrested and sent to prison for a while; I was

prepared to put up with that for the sake of achieving my

many wishes… so why am I so afraid? I don’t know why I

feel such a sense of mounting horror and cowardice. I see

myself as weak-hearted! But no… I’m not! I should control

myself. It is only for a short time… some days or months at

the most. Yes, I’ll be patient until it’s over.’

He continued to mutter these statements to himself to

relieve his fear and concern, but when he remembered that

— صفحة 146 —

Prisoner in the Castle or Guest of Honour?

145

his name was listed with those to be sent to the castle where

our officer Mohammad Emin was the director, he lost his

mind and became terribly anxious and confused once again,

‘But, will that man leave me alone? I don’t think so. No

doubt he’ll seize the opportunity to inflict all kinds of

torture on me because I wronged him and did my best to

outdo him and disgrace him. I’m sure that he won’t lower

himself to forgive me; of course he won’t, he’ll even use his

position to destroy me and to make me serve as a lesson for

everybody. Yes, I’m sure Officer Sheikho will use the lash

on me; he’ll probably shave my hair and pull out my nails.

My back will be ripped and he’ll scar my skin with his

cigarette butts… I’ll lose everything: my health, my youth

and my name.’

While enveloped in that black state of hysteria, a strong

feeling of dizziness overcame him and he felt as if the

ground shook beneath his feet. Wherever he moved he saw

his shadow following him, provoking him. He boiled with

uncontrollable rage and gnashed his teeth… and then he

walked slowly towards the wall to kill that black picture

and toss it on the floor. He thought that he could wipe it

out, so he kicked the wall, then punched it, but to no avail.

Finally, he found himself at the end of his tether, so he

surrendered to it and accepted its existence. He knew that

there would be no escape from his punishment and there

was nothing he could do except face up to it and patiently

bear his suffering.

— صفحة 147 —

Stories of the Scholar

146

‘It is my past history which I created by my own

actions… my own terrible deeds. I have done many bad

things in my life. Firstly I wronged myself and then I took

every opportunity to do evil and tell lies. How many nights

have I lain awake, planning and scheming? How many days

have I spent searching and asking? How many doors have I

knocked at? How many clubs and coffeehouses have I

visited so as to be on good terms with certain people and be

accepted by them? It is my own tongue which spoke the

words, and my pen which wrote them. Oh God! Isn’t there

any way for me to get out of all of this? Isn’t there any way

for me to feel at ease or to sleep? Oh God! Please help me; I

can’t stand up any more. Oh my God! Please show me

Your Mercy. I wish to God I had died before this disaster.

Death would be easier than the shame which I will feel

when I stand before Officer Mohammad Emin, in chains

and humbled, my eyes looking down.’

Before continuing this story, let us study the reason that

caused this guilty prisoner to suffer such deep anxiety and

terrible feelings, and the fearful prospect of the outcome

which he had drawn in his mind. Definitely, he knew that

he had been wrong and unjust, just as he knew for certain

that the reasons for his actions were certainly not good.

He remembered how he had stood against all that was

right in order to achieve his personal aims and gain

advantages. He turned to libelling the good reputation of

— صفحة 148 —

Prisoner in the Castle or Guest of Honour?

147

that pure man, Officer Mohammad Emin, and his social

standing among his superiors; furthermore, he tried to

implant doubts about his high honour and noble

intentions. He did all that because Officer Sheikho stood in

his way and stopped his wrongdoing.

Our officer feared no-one in his endeavours to establish

justice. He did not hesitate for a single moment in

performing all that his true love for God and his caring

about the advantages for His creatures inspired him to do.

He thought of himself as being in charge of protecting

people and helping them to follow the way of the most

beloved of all Prophets and the imam of all men, our pure

and great master Mohammad (cpth).

Therefore, our compassionate man, Mohammad Emin,

always refused all requests

2 made by such people because he

knew of the bad outcome for the person himself, as well as

for the whole of society in general. How many times had he

taken the side of the persecuted against those who unjustly

used their power and influence? So, through his mercy he

interrupted the course of the greediness of this man who

now became a prisoner, for Mohammad Emin cared about

what was right for him and refused his evil requests. Yet the

man regarded this as an insult, so he decided to fight him

and even try to kill him. But now, since this sinner had

2 The requests included encroachments upon others’ rights and grabbing their

lands and possessions by means of a bribe given to people of power. So, our

officer refused to agree to such requests, and he even fought against them.

— صفحة 149 —

Stories of the Scholar

148

admitted to himself that truly he was at fault and that all

his claims were baseless, and in fact it was his own whims

and lust which had engulfed him and made him lose sight

of the right way, he realised that the officer would be right

to punish him and take his revenge. This is what made him

so terrified and caused such fearful thoughts to flood his

imagination, to the point that he wished he could die rather

than meet face to face with Officer Sheikho, the general

manager of the castle and its prison.

In the meantime, the daily list of names of the new

prisoners arrived at the castle at the normal time, and

Mohammad Emin, as usual, sat at his desk in the director’s

office and began to read the list to see if he recognised any

of the names. Suddenly, a wonderful gleam came to his

pure eyes when he saw the name of a certain man. He knew

he was not wrong! He wondered about it, then said to

himself, ‘Oh you low life! So, your dirty wheels have run

their course and carried hundreds of losers with you,

clinging to your back! And here is one of those whom you

rejected and tore into with your claws! And now he’s to be

brought to my castle and come under my control which,

surely, never crossed anyone’s mind!’

So, this majestic, imposing castle is about to witness a

new battle with a prisoner who has been entrusted to the

merciful care of Officer Sheikho and will be enveloped in

his noble, superior intentions. Sweet tears of joy flowed

from the eyes of our noble officer as he breathed a deep,

— صفحة 150 —

Prisoner in the Castle or Guest of Honour?

149

fragrant sigh of relief, and his affectionate voice quivered

with statements of praise and immense gratitude directed

towards this Grand God Who was overwhelming him with

love and tenderness.

‘How Merciful You are, my God! Despite the fact that

he has distanced himself from You, and despite his fight

against right, and his wrong to himself, You did not close

the doors of love and forgiveness in his face… in fact, I see

him as more fortunate than anybody else as he is about to

receive a great share of Providence and good fortune. Who

would believe that fate has led him here? What a great

surprise! I think that he must be in a state of shock now.

He probably thinks that I am very happy because of his

situation and cannot wait to take my revenge on him. Poor

man! He may be trembling with fear, ashamed and

suffering from great anxiety. Oh what a poor man!’

Signs of Holy Love and Clemency appeared on

Mohammad Emin’s face while a pleasant smile appeared on

his lips expressing his pleasure and endless praise to God for

this opportunity which He had given to him.

Anxious to put his merciful plan into action, he called

the gendarmes, and in no time, three of them entered the

office. They were faithful to him and captivated by his

noble character which overwhelmed them with the great

care and interest he showed each of them. Countless times

he had helped them to live in peace, far from falling foul of

the danger lurking either within the castle or beyond it.

chapters.title: صفحة 151 - 160 (Stories of the Scholar)
chapters.html:
— صفحة 151 —

Stories of the Scholar

150

He told them, ‘Tomorrow, the castle will be honoured

by the visit of a man who is dear to us. I’ve decided to

receive him as a guest to spend some time here in our

castle. So, you have to prepare the best room in the castle,

paying particular attention to its location, outlook and size.

I want it to be furnished with luxurious furniture. Clean it

from top to bottom and paint the walls bright white. Don’t

forget to put pots of flowers and greenery in the corners to

brighten them. Ensure that it’s provided with every possible

convenience and good lighting by which he’ll be able to

relax both day and night. It will be a good idea to cover the

floor with beautiful, high quality carpets. In short, I want

you to prepare a wonderful room, and I want it to be

finished today. Off you go… quickly… and make sure that

the room is ready for receiving the important guest.’

They saluted him respectfully then rushed off to decide

which room would meet all the specifications listed by their

hospitable commandant. They divided the work among

themselves: one brought the paint and began to paint the

walls energetically while another started to sweep and wash

the floors.

When they had completed these preparations they went

to bring luxurious pieces of furniture and arrange them in

the room in the most elegant and comfortable way. And

finally, they brought the carpets and the planters containing

displays of greenery and beautiful roses which completed

the perfect overall appearance of the room.

— صفحة 152 —

Prisoner in the Castle or Guest of Honour?

151

And so, with the willing gendarmes put to work all was

accomplished within a few hours and everything was

arranged in the best possible way. Then, one of the

gendarmes headed for Mohammad Emin’s office to tell

him that the room was ready for his inspection and give his

approval. Our officer went up to the room which was

situated in the tower. During his inspection, he noticed a

few small imperfections that did not meet with his excellent

taste and exacting standards. Once these had been put to

right, he set off on his usual thorough inspection of the

castle and to check the conditions of the prisoners, to be

sure that all his orders had been carried out according to

the smallest detail. Then, this shining example of leadership

and dignity returned to his office and sat looking forward

to the arrival of the “special guest” so as to receive him

personally with great hospitality and all due attention.

Dear reader, do you think this is an exaggeration or that

it is just an ingenious trap set by the director for him to

sneer at this prisoner and then change his tactics to torture

him?

As for the prisoner, he spent a sleepless night, groaning

and suffering the most terrible bouts of fear. Whenever he

felt that the time to leave for the castle approached he

became even more anxious and alarmed. He felt as though

he was living a horrible nightmare from which he would

never wake up. With the dawn of the new day, he felt that

he could no longer think or feel anything. When the

— صفحة 153 —

Stories of the Scholar

152

policeman came to take him away he stretched his hands out

to be shackled and followed him with heavy, shuffling steps.

The patrol wagon was waiting beside the police station in

front of the court in al-Marjah Square, Damascus, and it was

filled with prisoners to be driven to the castle. His spirits fell

even further as he climbed in to join them.

The wagon trundled slowly on its way, laden with two

things: the exhausted hearts of the men it was transporting

and the huge wheels which, with every turn, drew ever

deeper lines in the hearts of those poor men that they

would never forget. In fact, it was they themselves who had

etched those lines through their own mean deeds which

had caused them this hardship. Every one of them was

looking through the bars of the wagon, their sorrow clear to

see as they bid goodbye to their freedom and the wonderful

light of day; as the wagon rolled ever closer to the citadel

they endeavoured to remember the sight of everything they

passed: houses and streets, people walking by, and leave

behind them the happy memories of their past.

But! What brought you to such a situation?

Do you not have eyes to see with?

Do you not have ears to hear with?

Has Al’lah not given you hearts for you to be aware of

reality?

Oh that poor son of Adam! When he is enjoying good

health and youth, he forgets that he is a weak creature who

cannot do without his Creator. He becomes conceited, full

— صفحة 154 —

Prisoner in the Castle or Guest of Honour?

153

of himself, and preoccupied with his wealth and youth so

he lives this life as he pleases, trying to gain people’s

gratification and not God’s Satisfaction. He follows only

what is to his own advantage, even if that makes him go

against what is right and rebel against high principles. And

so, he sinks ever deeper into a mire of dirt until the day

comes when God removes his will and his power in a blink.

On that day, he will no longer be able to do anything for

himself. He will be put in his coffin and then be carried on

sturdy shoulders to be driven to the grave, to return to the

soil from which he was created. Then, the list of his works,

good and bad, will be shown to him to throw him into a

pit of contrition and regret.

When the wagon reached the entrance of the castle, the

prisoners got down with pain in their hearts, their heads

bowed. They stood in a long line in the great courtyard

while gendarmes stood on both sides waiting for the list of

names to be read out: each prisoner would be assigned to a

particular, numbered cell where he would stay for the

period of his sentence. There were various types of prisons

in the huge castle depending on the different judgements

and sentences handed out. The cells in the tower were

usually assigned to those who had committed relatively

minor misdemeanors where the sentences were short-term

of one year or less. Those prisons were comparatively good

in comparison with the others, which were very harsh and

more effective on the spirits of the prisoners who were there

— صفحة 155 —

Stories of the Scholar

154

for long sentences, sometimes even with added penal

servitude, that is, “prisons within prisons”.

So, during his sentence, every prisoner had to pass

through various difficult circumstances until he became

used to a harsh way of life, the face of the jailer became

familiar to him, and he accepted loneliness as his only

constant friend until God’s Relief finally came.

After the list was read out, the prisoners were led by the

guards to their assigned cells. Some were taken to solitary

cells, others to collective ones. As for those sentenced to

death or to life or long-term imprisonment, that is people

who had committed serious felonies and acts of depravity,

they were taken to the castle, while the prisons in the

towers were the place for those who had committed simple

misdemeanours and offences.

When our prisoner heard his name called out, he sought

refuge in God.

He heard, ‘You, gendarme! Take him to his special

room.’

‘Special room?’ he thought, ‘What does that mean? Is it

a place where I’ll be singled out for torture?’

It was zero hour and he was about to meet him… that

officer!

He could not remember how many steps he mounted or

how many dark passages he passed through, but suddenly

he found himself before the door of that room which he

was certain would open to reveal all kinds of torments and

horror.

— صفحة 156 —

Prisoner in the Castle or Guest of Honour?

155

The warder opened the door… and he could only stand

and blink his sorry eyes! There was the most wonderful

room opening up before him: the sun’s rays came flooding

through its sparkling windows to fill the place with light.

Pots of brightly coloured flowers and abundant green plants

had been placed in an elegant arrangement. The sunlight

interacted with the verdure of the plants to create a

wonderful, relaxing feeling inside the room, while a

pleasant perfume refreshed the spirits and tickled his nose.

Beyond the windows could be seen some lively finches

playing together and chirping happily, signalling the tone

of the coming meeting.

Then, the prisoner took his first step into the room but

he was immediately suspicious. He expected to see the whip

waiting for him or the castle commander sitting there

looking forward to meeting him. But when he saw the

comfortable set up, once again he felt confused and

thought that he had fallen into a new whirlpool that he

would never escape from.

So, many thoughts rushed through his mind, ‘This is

what I expected and feared. He’ll come to see me here, in

his luxurious room. It’s your time, Officer, to take your

revenge and to subject me to the worst.’

He stood beside the door awaiting his fate, and began to

curse his life-style which had brought him there. Time

dragged on as he thought about what might happen next.

Unable to relax, he began to pace around the room; then he

— صفحة 157 —

Stories of the Scholar

156

stood leaning against the wall, or sat on a chair beside the

door. In each position, a different picture came to his

mind, and he flared up in anger. His heart began to race;

and his breathing became so rapid that his chest began to

pump up and down out of his fear of the unknown. He

stared fixedly at the door, on the alert for the slightest

sound or movement that would indicate the arrival of the

manager.

Suddenly, the sound of footsteps reached his ears. ‘He’s

coming… He’s close to the door… He’s holding the door

handle… oh God!’

Just then, the door was opened and with that the

prisoner felt that his head had burst open too. He took

such a deep breath that he became dizzy and his face turned

ashen as though he was dying.

Our officer, Mohammad Emin, appeared before him

with his face as bright as the sun; a gentle and tender smile

appeared on his lips, and a noble look came to his eyes.

He greeted the prisoner, ‘ “Al-Salamu alaikum wa

rahmatullah!” Welcome my brother; I am so glad to receive

you as a guest in this modest castle.’

He approached the prisoner, welcoming him and

encircling him with his mercy just as the heavens embrace

the earth and surround it.

The prisoner could not believe what was going on… he

had just been greeted in the most cordial manner! It had

not occurred to him to expect such a reception. He never

— صفحة 158 —

Prisoner in the Castle or Guest of Honour?

157

once thought that he might expect such compassion from

that man who now stood before him and overwhelmed

him, and tore the fear and hatred from his heart.

Within an instant, Officer Sheikho had brought him a

new sense of vitality and engulfed him with happiness and

tenderness. His limbs felt like the branches of a tree that

had been watered by blessed water that refreshed his spirit

and given it renewed life. Moreover, the splendour of the

room had not been complete until our officer entered and

his presence seemed to turn it into a small Paradise where

the two men sat beside one another talking face to face.

The prisoner was staring at the officer in amazement:

fully absorbed in a state of deep contentment.

‘I know that I am to blame… it’s my own fault that I’m

here now! I was full of hatred and contempt and intent on

committing any offence to achieve my own ends! No-one

forced me to do what I did… I chose to spend my life

following foolish whims that led me to commit every evil

and despise every favour and charity shown to me!

‘You’re such an important man, so why are you treating

me with such clemency and acceptance? What stops you

killing me and getting justice for yourself? By God! I

cannot find any reason why you should receive me as a

guest, as if I am your close friend.’

These were the thoughts going through his mind. He

tried to find just one plausible reason why the officer

should greet him with friendliness and extend such a warm

— صفحة 159 —

Stories of the Scholar

158

welcome to him; why had he overwhelmed him with the

care and concern which was gripping his heart and causing

the firebrand inside him to die little by little, to be replaced

by a spring of holy love and loyalty to him and to the

Grand Omnipotent God, ‘Oh God! All my love, my praise

and my passion are directed towards You for what You have

directed towards me.’

It was clear that the kind treatment he received from

Officer Mohammad Emin had brought joy to his heart and

stopped his bad feelings. It even led him to feel deep

remorse and to repent all his past evil actions. His spirit had

been full of envy and bitterness, and he had gasped for

personal advantage and material things, wishing to get

them at any cost. And now it seemed that all of that

negativity was behind him.

So, we see, quite clearly, that Mohammad Emin helped

him go ahead in the way of purity. That meeting was the

first step on the journey, and then it was followed by longer

and greater steps. He gave up many of his own rights and

pleasures for the sake of that man’s return to happiness. He

spent time with him, and filled it with pleasure and

kindness, and created a friendly atmosphere when in his

company. He brought him tasty dishes prepared in his own

home: all this to be sure that the man’s emotional and

mental state improved and that he was making progress on

the new journey which he had begun with him. This

journey would return the prisoner to the right direction in

— صفحة 160 —

Prisoner in the Castle or Guest of Honour?

159

order to adopt a new level of conduct for himself under the

Benefaction of the Glorious and Praiseworthy God.

Indeed, the prisoner looked forward eagerly to every visit

from Mohammad Emin and it seemed as though he had

begun to be infatuated by our officer. He wished that he

could stay with him all day and night to take in the sense of

love that he emanated, in order to quench the thirst of his

heart after the long dry years when he had turned away from

God and all His Benefits. During the days he spent in the

officer’s company, he lived a life full of affinity and closeness:

it was a noble love, laced with gratitude, which had banished

all evil intent and thoughts of sin from his spirit.

So, he understood the lesson that was given to him and

learned many things from the wretched condition he passed

through; he changed his mind about many things and decided

to turn his back on his previous life and do away with his

former despicable conduct. Therefore, God commuted his

sentence and ensured that he should be released on bail after

only twenty days. He came out of the prison with renewed joy

in his heart and determined to think differently. He was

delighted to enjoy his freedom and happiness once again, and

determined to enjoy what was his and not lust after what

rightfully belonged to others.

He said goodbye to the castle governor and thanked him

warmly for his wonderful hospitality and personal kindness,

as he knew that for the rest of his life he would be indebted

to Officer Sheikho for the great favour which he had done

for him.

chapters.title: صفحة 161 - 170 (Stories of the Scholar)
chapters.html:
— صفحة 161 —

Stories of the Scholar

160

Mohammad Emin prayed for him wholeheartedly and

wished him well for the rest of his life. He emphasised that

happiness and safety are achieved only by being illuminated

by God’s Light, by observing His Commands and Laws,

and by avoiding all those deeds that He prohibited. His last

words to the man were those of the prayer, “Praise be to

God, the Provider of all worlds.”

From that day on, that man adopted the right path. He

kept company with the people of truth and actively became a

kind and compassionate human being who wanted only

God’s Satisfaction. Before he was sentenced to prison, he

had done all that he could to misrepresent the illustrious

aims of our officer, but as soon as he was freed he took the

opposite line and did all in his power to assert that our

chivalrous man was true and honest, and that every word he

uttered was true and just.

In the Holy Qur’an, God says, “Goodness and Evil

cannot be equal. Repel evil with what is good: then your

enemy will become as close as an old and valued friend.”

3

This story brings to mind the memory of a great day during

the age of our highest ideal, our master Mohammad (cpth): the

day of the conquest of Mecca. On that day, the believers

entered the city as conquerers under his leadership (cpth).

He (cpth) marched towards the city at the head of a great

force of Muslims who had migrated from Mecca to

3 The Holy Qur’an, Fortress (Surah) 41, Explained (Fussilat), verse 34.

— صفحة 162 —

Prisoner in the Castle or Guest of Honour?

161

enlightened Medina to escape from the non-believers and

their evil leaders who had tried to put an end to his mission

and to kill those who believed in him and seize their

possessions. But God, the Almighty, aided His Prophet

(cpth) and the believers, and it was not just a conquest but a

great triumph that established the right of Islam and raised

its banner above all others.

So, when our beloved master (cpth) entered Mecca, he

stood before a gathering of the people and addressed them

saying, ‘How should I act with you? What do you expect

me to do with you?’

‘You are like a noble-minded brother to us, as was your

father,’ they replied. Then, in all modesty but in full command,

he said to them, ‘You can go. You are free.’

Although he was the ruler who controlled everything, and

although he surely had the right and the ability to take

revenge on behalf of the believers and to treat the non-

believers as they, the believers, had been treated, this was not

his purpose and he was far above such actions.

Therefore, they submitted to him and their hearts began

to tend towards that humane compassion which soon

overwhelmed them. Yet the noble man (cpth) did not stop at

that; he also allotted the spoils gained by the Muslim army

after their victory in the Battle of Hunayn

4 to the non-

believers. He gave each of them two hundred camels, while

4 The Battle of Hunayn took place shortly after the conquest of Mecca, and is

a decisive event in the history of Islam

— صفحة 163 —

Stories of the Scholar

162

he gave four hundred camels to Abu Sufyan who was their

leader. He (cpth) wanted to draw Abu Sufyan closer to

himself and remove all the enmity, bitterness, and darkness

that was generated in his heart.

Indeed, after that, Abu Sufyan, along with his descendants,

turned into beacons for Islam and became the champions of

truth who spread Islam all over the world during its golden age.

The Prophet (cpth) replaced evil with good, and hatred with

love, though he had no need of these people and there was no

reason for him to seek their friendship. But his actions sprang

from his unequalled truthfulness, wholehearted devotion, and

overriding desire to uplift mankind to the appropriate level

which makes them true men so that they fulfill the Trust placed

in them and become deserving of their eventual return to the

Gardens of Eternity.

God says, “Al’lah does call to the Home of Peace: He

guides whoever wishes towards a way that is straight.”

5

So, the enlightened Medina is not only that of al-Hijaz,

and the accomplishments did not stop after the departure

of the Prophet (cpth) from this world. There is also an

enlightened Medina here in al-Sham,

6 and glorious and

illustrious feats were also performed on its land and among

its people. He (cpth) said, “Seek al-Sham.”

And the Almighty called it the Holy Land for it is the place

where the Godly Messages came down and is the cradle of the

Prophets (cptt).

5 The Holy Qur’an, Fortress (Surah) 10, Jonah (Yunus), verse 25.

6 Greater Syria, which was comprised of Syria, Lebanon, Jordan and Palestine.

— صفحة 164 —

Prisoner in the Castle or Guest of Honour?

163

There, in your hands, is its soil; there, before your eyes,

is its sky; and there its people are alive: ask them if you do

not believe it!

The stones of Damascus Castle bear witness to his honour!

The affirmations of his good deeds are found the length and

breadth of Syria and are carried along on the waters of the

great River Euphrates.

So, why do we choose the difficult way? Why do we

enter a house by scaling the high walls, from where we fall?

Why do we not choose the simple and obvious way, and

enter a house through the door?

Perhaps our spirits are destroyed for one reason or another;

perhaps we feel we can no longer stand up: then we shall

spend the rest of our life creeping along the ground and

buried beneath its stones.

We have been created on this earth and surely we all shall

return to it. Whoever thinks that this earth is a permanent

abode or place of enjoyment is foolish.

It is true that we are mortals, but we have been granted

superior faculties and unrivalled powers of thought and reason

that help us to become illuminated by God’s Light. When

this is achieved, and only then, no-one will be given power or

control over us, and only then will our wishes correspond to

that which all the Prophets (cpth) have brought to mankind.

— صفحة 165 —

164

A Complex Story of Punishment,

Rebellion and Mercy

fficer Mohammad Emin held many important

military posts during the French Mandate over

Syria and Lebanon. At this particular time he was

in charge of the central prison of Damascus Citadel and held

the position of garrison commander.

Day by day, he went about his usual mundane duties but

was beginning to feel frustrated and bored with the daily

routine of office life; for it should be pointed out that

previously in his career he had been the hero of the battlefields

and accustomed to much excitement. It came as a welcome

relief when the army commander phoned him and ordered

him to prepare a squad of policemen under his leadership to

undertake a security tour of the villages of Eastern Ghutah

1

during the time of the Great Syrian Revolution.

On hearing this good news Mohammad Emin’s bad

mood lifted instantly and his spirits soared with happiness,

for he had been carrying out nothing but tedious office

1 An area in the suburbs of Damascus.

O

— صفحة 166 —

A Complex Story of Punishment, Rebellion and Mercy

165

work for the past fifteen days, and had not been charged

with any mission outside the citadel boundaries. It was not

in his character to enjoy office work for he had always been

a man of action and besides, as was mentioned, it went

against his nature to indulge in a life of ease and comfort.

He wasted no time and immediately sent for his adjutant

and ordered the expedition to be prepared. This was

accomplished without any further delay and he was eagerly

anticipating the troop’s departure, but just as he was about

to mount his horse with his usual vivacity and exuberance, a

soldier rushed up to inform him that the high commander

was on the phone wanting to talk to him.

From Mohammad Emin’s point of view it was not good

news, for the high commander asked him to remain on

duty at the citadel, while his adjutant, a first lieutenant,

would replace him to lead the expedition.

Our officer spoke to his superior officer in a friendly and

cordial tone because of the personal connection that they

had. This high commander was very fond of our officer and

had a high regard for him due to his magnificent deeds;

besides which he was a close friend of Mohammad Emin’s

brother, General Saleem, since the general had been a

superintendent of the military academy in Istanbul.

Mohammad Emin tried to persuade him to change his

mind and said to him in an amiable tone, ‘Oh sir, I’m feeling

quite vexed as I have been doing nothing but monotonous

office work for a long time and I feel as if my soul will leave

— صفحة 167 —

Stories of the Scholar

166

my body if I have to do it any longer. You know that I do not

like it… in fact I detest it, because, as you well know, I’m

much happier when I’m fighting for the security of our

country or patrolling on horseback: so I request that you let

me go out on patrol as you originally ordered and let my

adjutant stay on duty instead of me.’

But the commander insisted on his decision and all of

Mohammad Emin’s attempts aimed at making him change

his mind came to nothing, and his commander then put

friendship and cordiality aside and said in a frank, military

tone, ‘Officer, I am giving you a military command to stay

on duty at the citadel while your adjutant leads the

inspection expedition… Understood?’

At this our officer became very agitated and flared up

angrily saying, ‘Yes, sir! At your command!’ Slamming down

the receiver, he then stormed out of his office to tell his

squad there had been a change of plans and that his adjutant

would now lead the patrol to Eastern Ghutah.

He returned to his office overwhelmed by the fury

erupting inside him… there was no way to escape from it

or to control it. He called one of his soldiers and ordered

him to bring a big block of ice, and when it was brought,

he started to crush the ice with his teeth to try to cool down

and find some relief from his terrible anger. But it was no

use, he could not quell his rage!

There and then, he stormed out of his office, mounted

his horse and left the citadel heading for his house. He

— صفحة 168 —

A Complex Story of Punishment, Rebellion and Mercy

167

cared nothing about the repercussions of his actions due to

his overwhelming surge of anger, and he said to himself,

‘To hell with them and my position and the citadel!’

He pondered his situation as the sun was setting in a blaze

of flaming glory, carrying its brilliant light to the west to

beam on other places and other people. After a while, as the

dark legions of night gradually chased away the last lingering

light of the day, so did his fury steadily subside and his anger

disappear. Slowly he returned to his normal state of calm,

and was released from his own inner turmoil. As he began to

turn the thoughts over in his mind he realised the magnitude

of the great responsibilities placed on his shoulders, and how

he had walked away from his position without appointing

someone to take over his duties.

He knew that if anything unexpected happened with the

prisoners inside the citadel, he would bear full responsibility…

and he thought to himself, ‘At any rate… I should not have

behaved as I did when I was angry, so I’d better go back to the

citadel and get on with my work.’

There and then, he mounted his horse and went back to

his office in the citadel where he settled down to carry out

his duties. He began to attend to the paperwork that had

accumulated on his desk during the day, and as midnight

approached, the phone rang. His commanding officer was

on the line in a state of extreme anxiety because of his great

affection for Officer Mohammad Emin which was only

strengthened by the news of a dreadful catastrophe which he

had just received.

— صفحة 169 —

Stories of the Scholar

168

‘Are you there?’

Mohammad Emin replied, ‘Yes… I’m here… did you

not order me to stay here?’ he said bitterly.

The commander added, ‘I mean did you not go with the

expedition?’

He answered, ‘How could I go when you told me not to

go? Then you made it a military order so I had to obey.’

The commander said, ‘I thank God that you were not

with them… do you know what happened to the troop?’

‘No… no, I don’t…’ he replied.

The commander said, ‘As the expedition, led by its officers,

reached the village of al-Maliha in Ghutah (rural Damascus),

they were ambushed by the rebels. The entire force, including

the officers, have been captured, and so far we know nothing

about them… whether they’re still alive… or dead… we have

no idea what has happened to them. From the information

we have we know that the inhabitants of al-Maliha village

conspired with the rebels. They hosted the officers, received

them hospitably, gave them food and prepared beds for them.

Then, when the officers were asleep they took their firearms,

and the revolutionaries went in and took all of them prisoner.

And their fate is still unknown. This news was reported to us

by one of our spies in the village.

‘Now what do you have to say about what I did to

you… wasn’t it for your own good?’

Mohammad Emin answered him, ‘So… you had prior

knowledge about it, sir… and that’s why you prevented me

from going?’

— صفحة 170 —

A Complex Story of Punishment, Rebellion and Mercy

169

The commander replied terror-stricken, ‘I seek refuge in

Al’lah… no… no… far be it, and certainly not… I did not

know anything.’

Then the commander seemed to writhe with fear

because if it were true that he had prior knowledge of the

attack, it would mean that he was a partner in the

conspiracy and would certainly face execution.

Mohammad Emin said, ‘So, Al’lah is the Maker and it is

He Who prevented me from being subjected to this

impasse… not you.’

The General said, ‘Yes! Al’lah… Al’lah really is the

Maker… The words I spoke came from my lips… but in

truth they came from Him… they were His Words.’

At this point, let us go to al-Maliha village to see exactly

what happened there:

When the group of policemen first reached the village,

the inhabitants welcomed them warmly and received them

most hospitably.

That night, the soldiers were given accommodation in

various houses of the village and the officers were

accommodated individually, each one in a different house.

They undressed and put on their night clothes, hung their

holsters on hooks on the walls. But there was trouble

looming! After the guests went to sleep, feeling tranquil and

honoured, they fell into the trap that had been set for them

by the rebels, aided and abetted by the people of the village,

chapters.title: صفحة 171 - 177 (Stories of the Scholar)
chapters.html:
— صفحة 171 —

Stories of the Scholar

170

who came to capture the officers one by one. Taken totally

by surprise the officers could offer no resistance.

The officers were shackled with chains and their firearms

became easy pickings for the rebels. They were driven

barefoot and clothed in nothing but their pyjamas to the

town of al-Sweida on al-Arab Mountain – where the flame

of the great Syrian revolution was first sparked – to stand

before Sultan Pasha al-Atrash, the head of the revolution

there.

It is well known that the roads leading to al-Arab Mountain

are very difficult for the traveller because they are full of rocks

and thorns; and one must keep in mind that the captured

officers were in chains and forced to walk barefoot. Their feet

were in a terrible state, bleeding profusely, and all the while the

captives were being lashed repeatedly, causing severe pain.

The officer in charge of the expedition was treated worse

than the others and received the greatest share of the

lashing and humiliation. He was brawny and fat, and was

singled out by the leader of the rebel group for him to

torment personally. He repeatedly whipped not only his

back but other parts of his body, too, during the time it

took for them to reach al-Sweida. Every time the lash fell

on the adjutant’s back it was accompanied by obscenities

because of his corpulence, in spite of the fact that this

officer, one day, had tried to plead on his behalf when he

was being punished by Officer Sheikho. And now, that

criminal had forgotten the officer’s previous efforts on his

behalf and was subjecting him to such serious torture that

— صفحة 172 —

A Complex Story of Punishment, Rebellion and Mercy

171

he lost about half of his body weight by the time they

reached the rebel headquarters in al-Sweida.

After negotiations between the government of the French

Mandate and the revolutionary command the captives were

released in accordance with specific conditions which the two

parties had agreed upon.

Let us now return to that unfortunate officer who was

charged with leading the patrol in place of our officer,

Mohammad Emin, and his adverse position with the leader

of this rebel group which we have previously mentioned:

what, exactly, was that position?

We shall relate it from the beginning:

The captive officer was an adjutant to Officer Sheikho in

managing the citadel at the time. One day, the warders of

the citadel seized a prisoner – who later became the most

famous of the rebel leaders – and brought him to our

officer after he had been caught in the act of trying to

commit a hideous immoral offence with another man.

Once our officer heard of this deviation, and assured

himself that it was true, he seized him by the collar and

threw him to the ground in the citadel square in front of all

the prisoners; then he set about whipping him and kicking

him until the blood flowed from all parts of his body. Yet

even this was not enough to give vent to his terrible anger,

so he set about tearing the man’s skin with his teeth!

The adjutant felt such distress for the criminal that he

begged his officer repeatedly to stop tormenting him, to the

— صفحة 173 —

Stories of the Scholar

172

extent that he burst into tears of sorrow while our officer,

Mohammad Emin, deaf to all entreaties, completely

ignored him.

The adjutant pitied the criminal, but his great mercy

stemmed from the fact that he did not know that the painful

beating this criminal was suffering held mercy folded within

it, although it appeared to stem from great wrath. And why

should it not be so when the criminal is one of those whom

Al’lah denounced when He said, “For you practise your

lusts on men in preference to women: you are indeed a

people transgressing beyond all limits.”

2

Whoever oversteps the bounds of Al’lah’s Legislation must

be punished strictly, and indeed, the terrible torment now

being inflicted on that criminal at the hands of this pure,

chaste man is actually good and merciful as it is an attempt to

save him from the jaws of degradation, moral descent, and

sexual deviation. Otherwise, these terrible traits would cause

him to lose all the benefits that Al’lah has prepared for him in

the life to come, and would expose him to the greatest

chastisement in the Hereafter if he does not repent and

withdraw from his sinful ways. Therefore, it is vital that such a

person should be disciplined in order to make him understand

the error of his ways and make him repent. And besides, he

will serve as a lesson to anyone else who is tempted to commit

such an offence, and consequently the entire community will

learn from the same lesson too.

2 The Holy Qur’an, Fortress (Surah) 7, The Heights (al-A’raf), verse 81.

— صفحة 174 —

A Complex Story of Punishment, Rebellion and Mercy

173

Weeks and months passed as this low opportunist gradually

became affiliated with the aims of the great Syrian revolution.

This is a normal occurrence during any revolution or uprising,

for there will always be those people – whose aims are

removed from the true purpose of revolution – who sneak

into its ranks, but whose aims are to achieve nothing but their

own disreputable personal objectives using the principles of

revolution as the means to achieve false glory. How quickly

they attain their aspirations as they let no opportunity pass

without seizing it to ensure that they appear as most loyal and

sincere members of the revolution.

Consequently, they ascend through the levels of eminent

positions through which they achieve what they will fail to

attain when no longer part of it.

This is applicable to that despicable man who is now –

as we have seen – a notable leader of this group of rebels,

and the victim in his grasp is the same adjutant who cried

out of mercy for him and who is now a captive in his

hands. Does this position not seem contradictory?

But, in reality, it is not so… and the definitive proof is that

the mercy which the adjutant showed for the criminal was

based on sentiment and not rational thought, for he had no

knowledge of the wisdom behind the beating; and so it was of

no purpose to the adjutant when he came into the grasp of

this criminal who subjected him to all kinds of torture.

But as for our man Mohammad Emin, although he

inflicted a severe beating on the criminal, this was as a

— صفحة 175 —

Stories of the Scholar

174

mercy upon him, for his aim was to satisfy Al’lah and to

deter his wrongful and obscene behaviour. This aim led

him to being in a fortified castle that safeguarded him from

that criminal or, indeed, from anyone else who intended to

harm him, throughout his entire life.

His only purpose in life beyond the grand deeds and great

sacrifices he carried out, and which were marked by humanity

and mercy was but to satisfy the Great Creator and to save

His creatures, to keep them from falling, and to help them

even if that resulted in infuriating mankind; therefore Al’lah

helped him, supported him and preserved him – by force if

necessary – from falling foul of the enemies of all that is right,

and of personal enemies too, as we have seen in our story.

So, those who stay within the limits ordained by Al’lah

will be protected by Him, “Al’lah is the Best to give care,

and He is the Most Merciful of all those who show

mercy.”

3

3 The Holy Qur’an, Fortress (Surah) 12, Joseph (Yusuf), verse 64.

— صفحة 176 —

175

— صفحة 177 —

THE END

Praise is to God, the Provider of the worlds
